_what_this_is: The units of work for this store, as a board. Two levels, like the board this one is modelled on at sgraph.ai/en-gb/dev/workstreams/: the top board has one card per workstream and the column it sits in is derived from its own tasks, and opening a card gives that workstream's tasks in the same four columns. A workstream is never dragged — it moves because a task in it moved, which means the summary cannot disagree with the detail.
_how_to_add: A unit of work is an object in this file. The board, the counts, the rail badge and the per-workstream page are generated from it, and a build check fails the release on a task with a status this board does not have or a source that names a review that does not exist. Adding work is adding a line; there is no second place to update.

columns.label: Queued
columns.meaning: Written down and agreed. Nobody has started and nothing is waiting on it.

columns.label: Up Next
columns.meaning: The next thing in this workstream to be picked up.

columns.label: In Progress
columns.meaning: Being worked on now, in this release or the one being cut.

columns.label: Done
columns.meaning: Shipped and checked. A task here names the release it landed in.

sources.self: Found while building, by the build or by reading the diff
sources.memo: A memo from the project lead, kept verbatim at /admin/memos/

workstreams.title: Take money at all
workstreams.description: No payment rail is live. Every checkout_url in data/checkout.yml is empty, so the store can be walked end to end and cannot be bought from. This is the workstream that ends that, and the shape of it changed on 16 September: the rail is no longer an amount-only link, it is Stripe's own catalogue and a real customer record behind every order including the free ones.

tasks.title: Create the products in Stripe
tasks.description: Done by the project lead on 16 September. Six products, GBP, and the shape is theirs rather than the one this plan first guessed: the two upper levels are a DEPOSIT and a DELIVERY that sum to the price, so a buyer paying in full adds both lines and a buyer starting adds one. That is the store's own “a fifth now and the rest on delivery” as two rows instead of a rule somebody has to apply. The dashboard's CSV export is committed and the build reconciles against it every release.

tasks.title: Set customer creation to always, and prove it on a £0 order
tasks.description: The single setting most likely to be missed. Without it a hundred-per-cent order completes, the buyer sees a confirmation, and no customer record exists — which is the exact opposite of why this rail was chosen. Proof is a Customer visible in the dashboard after one free order, not a screenshot of the toggle.

tasks.title: Create the promotion codes over the three coupons
tasks.description: The coupons are done — 25, 50 and 100 per cent, created 16 September, all once, all reconciling against the percentages this store honours. Zero promotion codes exist, and that is the gap. A coupon carries the percentage; a promotion code is the string a person is handed and the thing a link can carry pre-applied. The seven strings in data/discounts.yml map onto these three — five at a hundred per cent, kept separate so an order record says which one produced it.

tasks.title: Enable promotion codes on every link, prefill where a code was leaked
tasks.description: A link with the field switched off refuses a valid code with no explanation and the buyer blames themselves. Where a page publishes a code as part of a journey, the link on that page carries it already applied.

tasks.title: Bring the return address onto this site
tasks.description: Shipped in v0.3.0. The success address is this site's own page for the level, so there is nothing to settle with another team. The two parameters are unchanged; what moved is the origin.

tasks.title: Stand up the checkout.session.completed webhook
tasks.description: The step that unblocks a first paid order at £50, £500 and £1,500. Listen to the session, not the payment: a hundred-per-cent order creates no charge, so a handler keyed on a succeeded payment sees every paid order and none of the free ones.
tasks.blocked: Runs off this site. This site is static and opens no connection.

tasks.title: Take one real £10 payment and read the receipt
tasks.description: Every sentence on the rails page about what a receipt says is unverified. This is the task that makes them checkable.

tasks.title: Retire the browser-side discount arithmetic
tasks.description: A code is honoured in the browser today and the page says it is a demonstration. Once a promotion code exists on the rail there are two implementations of one rule, and the browser one can be edited by the person it is discounting.

tasks.title: SumUp — parked for the MVP
tasks.description: Taken off the store on 16 September. The finding that produced this task — that check_checkout_links pinned every destination to Stripe's hosts and would have refused a SumUp URL with a message about Stripe — is now moot rather than fixed, and stays written down because it will be true again the day the rail comes back. The plan is kept at /admin/rails/sumup/ rather than deleted.

tasks.title: Write the two rails up as plans rather than intentions
tasks.description: Shipped in v0.1.18 at /admin/rails/stripe/ and /admin/rails/sumup/, generated from data/admin/rails.json.

tasks.title: Get the codes into Price.lookup_key, not just the description
tasks.description: The six codes exist as ABP-T1, ABP-T3-DEPOSIT and the rest — in the price description, because the dashboard's product view surfaces no lookup key. That works for a person reading the dashboard. Price.lookup_key is a different field, it exists on the API, and it is the one a webhook uses to map a line item back to a level. Without it the handler has a product id and a free-text string, which is workable and is not the same as queryable.

tasks.title: Re-export the product CSV whenever the dashboard changes
tasks.description: The reconciliation reads a committed export, because this site opens no connection and that rule is not moving. It catches a price changed here and not there, which is the direction that happens; it goes stale in the other direction until somebody re-exports. That is the known weakness and it is written on the page rather than left to be discovered.

tasks.title: Decide what a DELIVERY-only purchase means
tasks.description: The split makes a new thing possible that no page describes: somebody buying the delivery line without ever having bought the deposit. Either the pages say what that is, or the link only ever offers the pair.

tasks.title: Caps on the hundred-per-cent coupon — ruled not needed
tasks.description: Ruled on 16 September: no cap, and the reasoning is recorded rather than the concern being dropped. Purchases are managed directly, so a redemption is seen rather than discovered in a total. Abuse at a volume worth doing is abuse at a volume that shows. And what the code skips paying for is already published free — it removes a payment for material anybody could download, and it does not remove the work at the upper levels, which a person does and would notice. The gate now reports the state every release instead of failing on it.

tasks.title: Bring SumUp back once Stripe has taken money
tasks.description: The argument for running two rails is a good one and it is preserved on the parked plan. It stops being hypothetical the day the first rail has taken a real payment, which is the point at which there is something to compare against.

workstreams.title: The entry price, and what it buys
workstreams.description: Two reviewers independently said the entry level reads as a commodity at £5 — one human partner and one invented buyer who had never met them. The answer ruled on 16 September is not a larger number for the same thing: the level goes to £10 and gains a commercial licence, which is a different product rather than a dearer one.

tasks.title: Move the entry level from £5 to £10
tasks.description: Shipped in v0.2.0. £10, with all three moves of the price kept on the page.

tasks.title: Dual-licence the pack: CC BY public, commercial to the buyer
tasks.description: Shipped in v0.2.0. The public files stay CC BY; the buyer gets a commercial licence over the same material. The wording is not drafted and the ledger says so.

tasks.title: Research the cleanest way to grant it
tasks.description: The licence is to the buyer and does not name them, which is the interesting part: a grant to an unnamed holder has to be worded so it is clearly a grant and not a public re-licence of the same bytes. Open questions: does it travel with the file or with the order reference, what happens on resale, and does it survive the buyer's company changing name.

tasks.title: Put the licence text where the buyer reads it before paying
tasks.description: Not in the pack, not in a footer. The difference between the free version and the paid one is now the main thing the entry level sells, so it belongs on the card and on the level page above the fold.

tasks.title: Record the price arc as one claim, not three
tasks.description: The ledger already carries £10 → £5 with the card-fee arithmetic. Adding £5 → £10 as a separate claim would leave a reader assembling the story from three entries. One claim, three dates, all the reasoning kept.

workstreams.title: Who runs the review
workstreams.description: The two upper levels are somebody's work and the store has never said whose. A buyer spending £1,500 on a security review is buying a person, and the site asks them to buy it from nobody in particular. First reviewer named 16 September; the surface is built for several, because there will be.

tasks.title: Build the reviewer register and a page per reviewer
tasks.description: Shipped in v0.2.9 as data/reviewers.yml and /who/. Built for a list on the day it had one name on it — adding the second is adding a record; the page, the twin, the register entry and the links from the level pages are generated.

tasks.title: Write the first reviewer's page
tasks.description: Shipped in v0.2.9 at /who/dinis-cruz/. Every line read off open-source.sgit.ai's published author page and the vault catalogue, both named on the page with the date they were read. No count of years: the published record starts in 2008 and a reader can do that arithmetic and check every step of it.

tasks.title: Let the buyer choose their reviewer at £500 and £1,500
tasks.description: A selection, carried in the order reference the way the shape already is. With one reviewer it is a statement rather than a choice, and it is already on both level pages, because what it says is that there is a name behind the work.

tasks.title: Recruit the rest
tasks.description: The project lead is contacting security professionals they know and negotiating rates, so they can take some of the work at £500 and £1,500 and eventually above. The page is worth being listed on now, which was the whole reason WD-2 came first. Adding one is adding a record to data/reviewers.yml; the frozen list in the gate moves with it, on purpose, so a reviewer cannot appear by accident.

tasks.title: Say what happens when the chosen reviewer cannot take the work
tasks.description: Both upper levels already disclose they have never been sold. A named reviewer adds a second thing that can fail and the pages do not cover it.

workstreams.title: Leak the codes on purpose
workstreams.description: Seven discount codes exist and only the walkthrough page prints any of them. The ask is to publish codes on the main site on specific journeys — a code is a reason to complete a purchase, and a purchase is how a visitor becomes a customer record.

tasks.title: Decide which journeys carry a code
tasks.description: Answered by what the code can reach rather than by where it sits. The journeys are the two level pages the code applies to — /d/t1/ and /d/t2/ — because a code at the end of a level page discounts a decision somebody is in the middle of making, and a code on a first screen discounts one nobody has made yet. Not the home page.

tasks.title: Print the code on the journey, with the link carrying it applied
tasks.description: Shipped in v0.3.1. The code is printed and the same code is a one-click link that applies it and lands on the shop with the two prices repainted.

tasks.title: Give every leaked code a cap and an expiry before it is printed
tasks.description: Superseded by the ruling of 16 September: no caps, because purchases are managed directly and what this code gives away is already published free. What replaces a cap is stronger than one — the code cannot reach a level that is somebody's time, held by check_a_leaked_code_cannot_buy_somebody_s_day, which is absolute.

tasks.title: Keep the codes out of the built site except where they are meant to be
tasks.description: check_discount_codes_are_not_printed fails the release if a code appears anywhere outside /admin/. Extending it to a named set of journeys is a change to that check, not a hole in it.

workstreams.title: Close the loop after payment
workstreams.description: The store hands a buyer to riskmandate.ai and promises a person within 24 hours. Nothing carries the sale to that person, and nobody owns the mailbox it would arrive in.

tasks.title: Name the owner of the follow-up mailbox
tasks.description: Open since the 24-hour promise was written. It is one name and it is blocking nothing technical, which is exactly why it has stayed open.

tasks.title: Route the level-3 brief back to a person
tasks.description: At £500 the buyer writes a brief. It is a file they keep and there is no route by which the person doing the work receives it.

tasks.title: Verify the handover contract against a real landing
tasks.description: The store builds the address riskmandate.ai's pages document. Nobody has watched a real buyer arrive on one.

workstreams.title: Keep the record
workstreams.description: The reviews, the ledger, the console and this board. The part of the store that exists so a decision taken today can be argued with in a month.

tasks.title: Give the admin surface its own console UI
tasks.description: Shipped in v0.1.18. Rail, counts read from the same files the pages are built from, and a shell that is not the shop's.

tasks.title: Build this board
tasks.description: Shipped in v0.1.18 at /admin/work/, modelled on the workstreams board at sgraph.ai. Three boards: this one authored, and two generated from the reviews and the ledger so they cannot drift.

tasks.title: Link the admin console from the main site's top-level nav
tasks.description: It was reachable only by knowing the address. Public and unadvertised was the intent; unfindable by the people building it was not.

tasks.title: Build the memo queue
tasks.description: Shipped in v0.1.18 at /admin/memos/. A memo is kept verbatim, read into a brief, broken into units of work, and the units appear on the board carrying the memo they came from. Set as the process by the memo it is generated from, and applied backwards to the two before it.

tasks.title: Operationalise the review proposals
tasks.description: Eighteen proposals across two reviews, each with a stance. The ones marked do-now are units of work and were not tracked anywhere until this board existed. The generated proposals board is the join.

tasks.title: Capture the next review
tasks.description: The register takes a file and a line. The interesting one to run next is a second synthetic pass after the rail is live, because every finding in the first one stopped at a checkout that did not exist.

tasks.title: Execute the memos in sequence, pushing often
tasks.description: Set as the working method: catalogue each memo exactly, plan, then execute bit by bit and keep pushing to production. Minor versions for most of it; a major version where a change is big enough to deserve one.

tasks.title: Join the memos to what they became
tasks.description: Shipped in v0.3.6 at /admin/status/. The queue said what arrived, the board said what it became and the release history said what shipped — and no page put the three together, so the only way to answer “what happened to that memo” was to read three pages and hold the join in your head. Every done unit now carries the pages it produced and the release it went out in, and a check refuses one that claims to be done and points at nothing.

workstreams.title: Qualify who is reading
workstreams.description: The store shows four paid levels identically to whoever arrives, which sells to everybody and therefore to nobody. Five audiences — founders, investors, C-level executives, cybersecurity professionals, and risk and governance or GRC professionals — each with its own path and its own subset of the offers. The front door stays exactly as it is.

tasks.title: Decide what happens to the three buyer groups
tasks.description: The store already has three, cut by situation rather than by role, each with a page in the nav and in the sitemap and claims citing them. Five new ones is a replacement and the memo does not say whether the old three are retired, re-cut or kept alongside. Nothing else in this workstream can start without the answer.

tasks.title: Write the five audiences down as data
tasks.description: Shipped in v0.2.7 as data/audiences.yml. One record per audience: who they are, what they arrive asking, which level the view leads with, which are quieted, and the one published vault that speaks to them.

tasks.title: Hidden, or shown differently — answered
tasks.description: Shown differently. Nothing is hidden from anybody. Each view leads with the level that usually fits the question somebody arrived with and quiets the ones that usually do not; every level stays present, reachable and priced on every view. The alternative would have meant this site showing different catalogues to different readers, which is a thing that has to be said out loud before it is built. check_the_five_audiences_hide_nothing is what stops quiet quietly becoming absent — that change is one CSS rule away and would look like a tidy-up in a diff.

tasks.title: Build the five paths
tasks.description: Shipped in v0.2.7. Five paths at /are/, generated — a sixth audience is a file.

tasks.title: Run a synthetic pass over the five paths
tasks.description: Named in the memo as the feedback loop for this work. The method exists and has been run once; the second run is the one that tells us whether it generalises.

workstreams.title: The version the board can read
workstreams.description: “Can I have this in a form my board can read?” Every vault should already contain one — the policy re-cut for the people who have to sign it off. Not a paid extra and not an add-on: every vault, including the ones anybody can download for nothing.

tasks.title: Specify what a board-readable cut actually is
tasks.description: Length, what it leads with, what it leaves out, and what a reader is expected to do with it. It is the whole deliverable, so specifying it badly is worse than not shipping it.

tasks.title: Decide who writes it, per vault
tasks.description: Fifteen shapes. Generated, written once per shape, or written per sale — the answer changes what the entry level costs to fulfil and therefore whether £10 is the right number.

tasks.title: Say on the site what is inside a vault
tasks.description: The memo's own diagnosis: the store never explains this well. It is the gap the board-readable cut sits in, and it is worth closing on its own even if BR-1 takes a while.

tasks.title: Put it in the free vaults first
tasks.description: “Including the ones you can download for free.” Doing the free ones first is the harder order and the right one: it proves the cut is generated rather than hand-finished for a paying customer.

tasks.title: Re-read the entry level once it carries one
tasks.description: A £10 pack that contains a version the board can read is a different argument from a £10 pack that does not. It also earns a row on the comparison table, which is where the difference between the levels is now legible — and it is kept off that table until it exists.

workstreams.title: Decouple the views
workstreams.description: Five audiences across the surfaces they touch is not writeable by hand. The store is already data-driven at the content layer and hand-written at the view layer, and that seam is what the memo is pointing at: JSON configuration, components, and the same generate-and-check discipline coding.sgit.ai and nfrs.sgit.ai both teach.

tasks.title: Read the two guidance sites properly and write down what applies
tasks.description: coding.sgit.ai measures its conventions by counting the code rather than asserting them; nfrs.sgit.ai runs one rule — link the measurement, never restate it, generate or date every number — and fails its build otherwise. This store already runs both of those; what is not yet written down is which of their component conventions apply to a site that ships no framework.

tasks.title: Settle: custom elements at runtime, or generated partials at build?
tasks.description: This is the decision the rest depends on and it has a hard constraint on it. Every selling page on this site opens no connection and a build check fails the release if one does. Components that fetch their own configuration would negotiate with that rule. Components that are rendered at build from the same JSON would not, and would still give the memo what it asked for.

tasks.title: Lift the view layer out of build.py into declared blocks
tasks.description: Three thousand lines, of which the page shells and the block renderers are the part five audiences would multiply. Extract those first; leave the markdown renderer and the gate alone.

tasks.title: One JSON file per view, and a check that fails on an unused one
tasks.description: The store's own idiom, applied to views: a register with no file and a file with no register entry both fail the build, the way the reviews already do.

tasks.title: Prove it by adding the sixth audience as a file
tasks.description: The acceptance test for the whole workstream. If adding an audience is still a code change, the refactor did not land.

workstreams.title: Never leave the site
workstreams.description: A buyer does the whole thing here — catalogue, cart, payment, receipt, and the vault they just bought, embedded on the page they land on. Today the store hands them to another domain at the moment they pay, which a synthetic buyer called out as the point they got confused.

tasks.title: Narrow the no-network rule before the first cross-origin read
tasks.description: Done in v0.3.3, with a consumer rather than on spec. The no-network rule was narrowed a second time to admit the vault embed on the page a buyer lands on. The half that carries the claim did not move: every page that SELLS anything opens nothing at all, and there is now a check that refuses an embed on one by name. Five deliberate breaks run.

tasks.title: Move the post-sale page onto this site
tasks.description: Shipped in v0.3.0. /paid/t1/ to /paid/t4/ are on this site: the order reference filled from the browser that placed it, what was bought, when it arrives, who does it, what done looks like and how to check it. Every page noindex, and correct with no script at all — a browser that blocked it still reads what happens next.

tasks.title: Embed the bought vault on the page they land on
tasks.description: Shipped in v0.3.3. The three levels that are a vault embed a published one on the page after payment, labelled an example, not yours in its first sentence — because at the moment somebody pays there is nothing of theirs to show yet, and a page that pretended otherwise would be lying at the one moment a buyer is paying most attention.

tasks.title: Read riskmandate.ai's manifest over CORS and close the last hop
tasks.description: Blocked on the brief, and now for a named reason. Their manifest exists — fifteen entries with bytes and a sha256 — and it lives inside a JavaScript const DIST = /*__DIST__*/[…] in paid-t1.html, not at a JSON address. Reading it means regex-ing their JS out of their HTML at runtime, which is exactly the fragility item one of the brief on /boundary/ asks them to remove. CORS is confirmed; the shape is the gap.
tasks.blocked: The RiskMandate team publishing a manifest as JSON — item 1 of the brief.

tasks.title: Make the store feel like a shop
tasks.description: “Fundamentally like Amazon.” More detail is coming from the project lead. Several pages here are an essay with a buy button under them, which is the gap.
tasks.blocked: More information from the project lead.

tasks.title: Re-run the synthetic buyer who got confused
tasks.description: The finding has a name and a persona attached. The same walk, after the flow is one site, is the only way to know this worked.

workstreams.title: Who owns what
workstreams.description: Two sites, one purchase. The store owns e-commerce — cart, workflow, redirections, payments. riskmandate.ai owns the products, the policies, the information and the screenshots. Written down where both sides' agents can read it, because a boundary nobody published is a boundary that moves.

tasks.title: Publish the ownership boundary as a page both agents can read
tasks.description: Shipped in v0.3.2 at /boundary/ — indexed, with a markdown twin, in llms.txt, so another team's agent can find it. The store owns e-commerce; riskmandate.ai owns the products and the material; the reader never crosses the seam.

tasks.title: Brief the RiskMandate team to do the reverse
tasks.description: Shipped in v0.3.2 as the second half of /boundary/: four asks in the order that makes each one useful on its own, and an explicit list of what is NOT being asked for — no callback, no session, no shared state, no account. Status open, and it will be recorded there when it is answered including if the answer is no, because a brief that only appears when it succeeds is a brief nobody should trust.

tasks.title: Mark the files that are on the wrong side
tasks.description: Done in v0.3.2. The one file on the wrong side is named on /boundary/ with what makes it survivable: data/abp-catalogue.json is promoted at build time with the source URL, the retrieval time and a sha256, so it cannot drift silently. It is still the wrong arrangement and the page says so.

tasks.title: Agree the contract for the shared files
tasks.description: Both directions need a stable address, a stable shape and a version field — three different promises, all three needed. CORS makes the read possible; it does not make it safe to depend on. Asked for as item four of the brief on /boundary/.

workstreams.title: The comparison table
workstreams.description: Features down the left, five columns across — free, £10, £50, £500, £1,500. The page that makes the differences between the levels legible, and the one that finally explains the entry price, because a licence is only a difference next to a column that does not have it.

tasks.title: Decide what every cell is allowed to say
tasks.description: Answered by building it the other way round. A row goes on the table only when each of its five cells can be pointed at — a price in data/offers.yml, a gets sentence, a not-promised line, or a ruling. A row whose cells would be a promise is not on the table at all. Fourteen rows qualified.

tasks.title: Write the feature list as data
tasks.description: Shipped in v0.2.8 as data/comparison.yml. Fourteen rows in four groups, each carrying the sentence that says what the reader is actually buying.

tasks.title: Settle whether £10 includes a vault
tasks.description: Settled by reading what the level already says. £10 is explicitly not a vault — its own page has said so since it was written — and £50 is where a vault starts. It was never a proposal; it was already true.

tasks.title: Decide what support means, and who answers
tasks.description: Deliberately kept off the comparison table until it is decided. Email support on the paid levels was floated in the memo and never scoped. What is true today and could be said instead: every purchase is managed directly by the person who does the work. That is stronger than a support tier and it is also a different promise, so it needs saying on purpose rather than by default.

tasks.title: Build the page, free column first
tasks.description: Shipped in v0.2.8 at /compare/, free column first.

tasks.title: Render it as a PDF
tasks.description:
Done. tools/make_pdfs.mjs renders the real page through the real print stylesheet, so nothing is retyped — a row added to data/comparison.yml is in the brochure on the next run. A4 landscape, because five columns and a wide row label do not fit portrait without shrinking the body copy past reading at arm's length. Six sheets: four of table, two of the explanation under it.

It is not in the gate, for the same reason as the walkthrough and the concept screenshots — it needs a browser, and the gate is Python and node --check with nothing installed. So the drift is checked instead: the file still has to hash to what the tool recorded, its version has to be one this site really released, and a copy that lags the current release is a note rather than a failure, with the page printing the version beside the link.

workstreams.title: Product pages that show the product
workstreams.description: “We go there, we don’t know what we’re buying.” Description, price and a buy button, a carousel of what you actually get, specs and SKUs, and a place for reviews. Prototyped in the lab first, reviewed, then wired in.

tasks.title: Prototype one product page in the lab
tasks.description: Shipped in v0.3.4 at /lab/product/ — in the surface that already protects it, because a page that looks like a shop and is not one is the most dangerous thing this site could publish and /lab/ says so on its own face with a check behind it.

tasks.title: Find out which screenshots exist and which have to be taken
tasks.description: Counted: seven screenshots exist, of which three are of this store's own screens and usable. The prototype has seven slots and the four empty ones say what belongs in them.

tasks.title: Put a version on every piece of product media
tasks.description: A product page is where a store goes stale first. Four of the seven slots are empty and named; the three that are filled carry no version, and the walkthrough PDFs already put one in the filename for exactly this reason.

tasks.title: Print the specs and the SKUs
tasks.description: The store has 62 and shows none. The same data the Stripe rail is about to need.

tasks.title: Add the review section, and say it is empty
tasks.description: Done in the prototype: the section says there are none, says what will fill them, and says there will be no star average, now or later — a rating out of five on a product nobody has bought is the one piece of furniture on that page that could not be honest.

tasks.title: Make the page switchable by audience
tasks.description: Shipped in v0.3.4 as a first cut: five edition buttons that change one sentence. The open question is on the page — whether an edition should change the pictures too, which is what would make it an edition rather than a label.

workstreams.title: What has actually been done
workstreams.description: The store says the upper levels have never run for a paying buyer. True, and it reads as “nobody has ever done this”, which is false. The work has been done many times and published; what has not happened is a sale through this checkout. Lead with the first, keep the second, stop letting one stand for the other.

tasks.title: Re-read every claim against “the work has been done”
tasks.description: Fifty-two claims re-read one at a time in v0.2.1. The offer states, the ledger's own legend for specified-never-run and the home page's headline sentence were wrong as written; the rest were precise and were being misread.

tasks.title: Link the published evidence
tasks.description: Shipped in v0.2.1. data/evidence.yml carries six published vaults, quoted from the catalogue that generates them, on the home page. Every URL returns 200 and a check holds them to the domain that publishes them.

tasks.title: Narrow the disclosure to what is genuinely undone
tasks.description: Shipped in v0.2.1. The disclosure now says what is true: a first buyer is the first through this checkout, not the first to have the work done.

tasks.title: Put a name and a track record on the delivery
tasks.description: Twenty years of cybersecurity, in the project lead's voice with a source rather than asserted in the shop's. Same page as the reviewer work.

tasks.title: Decide what to do about testimonials
tasks.description: Asked for, and there are none. The review pages are critiques, which is a different object. A placeholder saying it is empty is the house style; an invented one would undo the rest of this workstream.

workstreams.title: Say when it arrives
workstreams.description: Every level gets an estimated delivery, because a shop that will not say when something arrives is a shop people leave. The numbers were given: immediate, one to two days, one to three days from receiving the customisation, one to five days.

tasks.title: Put a delivery estimate on every level
tasks.description: Shipped in v0.2.0, frozen in the gate beside the prices.

tasks.title: Replace the it-has-never-run non-answer about timing
tasks.description: Shipped in v0.2.0. The claim that said there was no measurement to quote now carries an estimate labelled as one.

tasks.title: Say what the constraint really is
tasks.description: Shipped in v0.2.0. The constraint is named as one person's calendar.

tasks.title: Start measuring the moment there is something to measure
tasks.description: An estimate becomes a record the first time an order runs. The ledger is built for exactly this.

workstreams.title: The homepage sells
workstreams.description: A counter at an event, not an essay with a buy button. Laptop or tablet turned round: who are you, here is your thing, buy it. Products up front, big targets, few of them, and everything about the mechanism moved to the admin side.

tasks.title: Move the mechanism and the meta off the front page
tasks.description: The home page opens by explaining what an Agent Behaviour Policy is. A shop opens with what is for sale. The explanation does not get deleted — it moves.

tasks.title: Put the four products up front, with prices and delivery
tasks.description: The thing being sold, visible without scrolling, with what it costs and when it arrives.

tasks.title: Build the who-are-you entry
tasks.description: Shipped in v0.2.7. Five doors on the home page and at /are/, five across on a laptop, two on a tablet, one on a phone. One tap to a view that opens on the level that fits.

tasks.title: Make a discount code a link, never a thing to type
tasks.description: “Click a link, apply the discount code.” The store already reads a code off the address and strips it from history; what is missing is the links.

tasks.title: Add the sections a shop front has
tasks.description: Feature sets, articles, end-to-end flows, testimonials. Asked for by name. Testimonials are blocked on there being any.

tasks.title: Test it the way it will be used
tasks.description: On a tablet, held, by somebody standing next to a stranger. Not in a desktop browser at 1440px.

tasks.title: Rename level four to match the product
tasks.description: Done in v0.2.4. The store now says “Two sessions and a custom vault”, following the project lead's rename in Stripe — it says what the buyer ends up holding rather than what happens to it. The professional signing it is on the level's own page, where it is a property of the thing rather than the name of it.

workstreams.title: Describe your agent
workstreams.description: A free page where somebody builds their agent by clicking or dragging capabilities onto it, and what comes out is a definition of what that agent could do — a document a model session can turn into a vault. It is the elicitation half of the £500 level, given away, and the project lead expects it to be the page they use most in conversation.

tasks.title: Get the real capability vocabulary
tasks.description: Got, rather than invented. Twenty-three primitives on a verb.object.reach grammar, read out of riskmandate.ai's own template vault with its published read key and promoted by tools/promote_capabilities.py with the hash of the bytes. The ultimate source is what-can-it-do.games.sgit.ai — one of the games the memo was pointing at.

tasks.title: Prototype the canvas — agent in the centre, capabilities around it
tasks.description: Shipped in v0.3.5 at /lab/agent-canvas/. All nine families on one screen, click to give a capability to the agent, click again to take it away.

tasks.title: Prototype the sequence — one question at a time
tasks.description: Shipped in v0.3.5 at /lab/agent-sequence/. Same twenty-three primitives, one family per screen, with what each reach means.

tasks.title: Decide whether a capability has degrees
tasks.description: Partly answered by the vocabulary itself, and the rest is still open. Degrees are not on the capability — send.endpoint.allowed and send.endpoint.world are two separate primitives, which is how “partially connect to the internet” is already expressed. What is not decided is whether the interface should also carry the barrier taxonomy, where only one of four kinds of restraint is actually a control.

tasks.title: Emit the definition as a document a model can act on
tasks.description: Shipped in v0.3.5. Markdown to the clipboard or JSON to your downloads, carrying the grammar and the reach glossary with it so the session reading it does not have to guess what world means. Nothing is sent anywhere and a check refuses a fetch in that file.

tasks.title: Write the prompt that turns the definition into a vault
tasks.description: A model session with the template vault takes the document and produces the buyer's vault. The store already ships a level-three prompt; this is its front half.
tasks.blocked: DA-8, and a decision on which of the two interfaces is real.

tasks.title: Say on the page what it is and is not
tasks.description: Shipped in v0.3.5, and held by a check: every prototype has to say it produces the grant only. A reader who thought this was the whole document would be taking three quarters of the £500 level for nothing in their own head.

tasks.title: Put it in front of the £500 level and in the walk-through flow
tasks.description: Free, in front of the paywall, and the thing a conversation at a stand is run from: build it together, they leave, the vault follows.

workstreams.title: Take the moves from the concepts
workstreams.description:
Three homepage directions arrived from outside on 16 September, drawn by a ChatGPT session from the live page. Two of them carry structure worth taking. This is that structure, broken into units, with what each one costs us written on it — because a borrowed idea whose price is not written down gets adopted and then quietly reverted. The critique is at /admin/concepts/ and the panel that tested the same four folds on five readers is at /admin/reviews/2026-09-16-four-homepages/.

NOTHING HERE OUTRANKS THE BUY BUTTON. Both the critique and the panel reached the same conclusion by different routes: neither the live store nor any concept has one, and a better shop window on a shop that cannot take money is worth less than the till. take-money stays first.

tasks.title: Ship the four-fact strip, every fact linked to its claim
tasks.description:
From 01 Marketplace, corrected by the one reader who checks things. Four short statements between the hero and the first product section: fifteen application templates, four levels, six vaults open to read now, the top two signed by a person. Every one of the four is already true here and already in the ledger.

Each item links to its claim. The concept's version has four ticks and not one of them is a link, which is the difference between a trust strip and a claim — and the reason this store can ship the idea and the concept could not.

tasks.title: Set the price at 42px on every card
tasks.description:
The live card sets the price at 28px inline with the delivery estimate, at body weight. Every concept sets it at 42px as the second-largest thing in the card, and every reader shown that version used the prices to compare.

A type-scale change, not a redesign. It is the measurable difference between a card somebody compares and a card somebody reads.

tasks.title: Rebuild the card anatomy: level and delivery on one line, one action
tasks.description:
Identical order in every card so the eye can run down a column: level and delivery on one 12px line, the name, one line of what it is, the price, one sentence, one action.

The claim chips have to go somewhere. They are load-bearing — they are how a reader checks that “delivered by a person” is a thing somebody stood behind, and they are one of the two elements that won the two readers who would spend the most. This is a move, not a deletion.

tasks.title: Applications as chips, with a sixth that converts the miss
tasks.description:
From 02 Guided, which lost the panel four-one and won this outright. One pill per application, each a link, with a sixth reading “something else — from £500”.

A visitor whose agent is not in the list currently reaches the end of a directory. The sixth chip sends them to the level that exists precisely because their deployment is not the template.

tasks.title: Forty-eight header links down to four
tasks.description:
The review's first recommendation and the right one. Three destinations and the order stay in the header; eleven evidence and buying-mechanics destinations move to the footer; eight already have a home in the console.

Two things do not move. The version badge is how a reader knows which build they are quoting, and the model-assistance strip is required above the main element by this repository's own rules with a check that refuses a page without it. They can get quieter. They cannot go to the footer.
tasks.blocked: TK-6, which changes the same fold

tasks.title: Cut the disclosure strip to one line without moving it
tasks.description:
It is two lines on a phone before the headline starts, and the headline starts 358px down. One line with the rest behind the link is the same disclosure at a third of the height.

It stays above main. It is one of the two elements that won the two readers who would sign off £1,500, and a build check holds the floor, so the failure mode is loud rather than silent.

tasks.title: A short name and a precise subtitle, in the same card
tasks.description:
Ruled on 16 September, by the project lead, out of the v3 design round. Pack, Vault, Tailored, Reviewed — a short name at heading size with the precise line underneath, which is the anatomy the design brief proposed rather than a choice between the two.

They live in data/offers.yml as short_name and short_sub beside the price, and check_next_is_the_offer_data holds both /next/ pages to them: a name that drifts from that file fails the release, which is the point of a name a buyer repeats to their board.

tasks.title: Decide what replaces “a licence to operate”, or that nothing does
tasks.description:
Raised twice, independently. The outside review flagged that “licence to operate” can be read as regulatory permission unless something beside it says otherwise; the panel found “powerful agents, clear boundaries” was the only headline every reader understood on sight.

Neither settles it, and nobody misread the live headline. It is also the name of a document inside the vault, so changing it on the homepage alone splits the vocabulary. A ruling, not a change.

tasks.title: Correct the £5 on riskmandate.ai
tasks.description:
A live defect, found from outside. This store prices the pack at £10 and riskmandate.ai's homepage still carries “1 · £5 The pack, downloaded”. The price moved on a memo from the project lead and the product site was not moved with it.

A buyer who reads both properties — which is the whole point of them being one flow — sees two prices for one thing. It is the other team's file to change, so it goes to them as a correction rather than a suggestion.

tasks.title: Show one real reader the same four folds
tasks.description:
The one thing that would outweigh the whole panel. Five invented readers cannot tell you what a stranger does, and the weakness is not the sample size — it is that the sample and the thing being sampled have the same author. A bigger panel scales the problem rather than the evidence, and is recorded as won't-do on the review so nobody reads the silence as a plan.

One person who has never seen the store, shown the same four folds at the same two sizes and asked the same six questions.

tasks.title: Rule on the mission line the v3 design carries
tasks.description:
The one section of the chosen design that is not built. The v3 pages carry a mission line under the heading why RiskMandate exists that uses a word this site bars absolutely, on every page, with no allowlist and no carve-out for a quotation — because a positioning phrase is a claim, but a priced checkout is an offer, and every page here carries a price.

Their own notes page records that the project lead asked for that line. So this is a collision between two things somebody is right about, and it is not the builder's to settle. Three ways out: the line stays off store.sgit.ai and lives on riskmandate.ai instead; or it is rewritten to say the same thing in words a priced page may use; or the rule is changed, which is a bigger decision than one section.

Recorded at /admin/next/ rather than silently dropped.

tasks.title: Build the rest of the next store, and wire the flow
tasks.description:
Two pages of the next store exist: the homepage and the product page. The cart, the checkout, the post-purchase page, the policy picker and the comparison are waiting on the next design round, and the buying flow is not wired at all.

That is the order it was asked for. When the next set of designs lands, the component layer and the data model are already there — assets/next.css and assets/next.js were written for the whole flow rather than for two pages.
